source.title: Causal dictionary learning reveals and validates transcription-factor binding features in genomic language models

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that individual neurons in genomic models are polysemantic and presents sparse-dictionary features as an alternative, but it does not measure neuron poles or test any listed version. Its binding-feature ablation results concern SAE directions, not neurons.
record.gate_note: The paper does not audit neuron poles, estimate the share of neurons with one or multiple jobs, evaluate explanations on held-out activations, or test neuron-based attribution graphs. Its own results concern causal validation of SAE dictionary directions for transcription-factor binding; these are recorded as findings about an alternative representational unit, with versions set to none. Background statements about neuron polysemanticity and cited findings are not recorded as result rows.
record.test_reason: The study never measures individual neurons. It asserts, citing Toy Models of Superposition, that genomic-model neurons are polysemantic and uses top-k SAEs as the remedy. All its results concern SAE dictionary directions in two DNA models (NT v2, DNABERT-2): motif enrichment, GC-matched binding sensitivity and causal ablation. It gives no neuron-pole shares, no neuron explanations scored on held-out data, no InceptionV1 analysis and no neuron attribution graphs. The record's T5 is wrong: the paper offers no results or specific argument against any version, only a background assumption opposite to the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that composition-matched testing plus causal ablation validates SAE features for TF binding across two architectures and three factors, with clean nulls under negative controls. They also conclude that naive PWM enrichment is confounded by GC content and repeats.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains top-k sparse autoencoders on genomic-model activations, composition-matches binding windows, and ablates dictionary directions; it does not audit individual neuron poles.
record.method_sensitivity: Dictionary reconstruction and live-feature fraction peak at intermediate depth; NT layer 14 and DNABERT-2 layer 6 were selected for subsequent analyses. The paper also reports differences in motif-selective feature counts across factors and architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: In NT v2 (layer 14) and DNABERT-2 (layer 6), ablating the top 15 binding-sensitive, GC-robust SAE directions gave binding-specific causal effects for 7-14 of 15 features per transcription factor. Random-feature controls gave 0/15, and scrambled-label controls yielded no binding-sensitive features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionary features in genomic language models can be causally validated as representing cell-type-specific TF binding. This concerns dictionary directions, not neurons.

record.problems: The study covers two masked-language-model encoders and three transcription factors; its authors note that autoregressive and state-space genomic models and broader factor coverage remain for future work. The recorded causal counts concern SAE directions, not neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Negative-label controls are described as yielding zero binding-sensitive features and therefore having nothing to test in the causal-ablation stage; they are not reported as causal-ablation outcomes.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or shares of one-job, two-job or not-yet-understood poles.
No neuron-pole shares in any language model, dense or MoE, at any scale. The DNA models are studied only through SAE features.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis and no test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No interpretable-neuron shares under different tools or architectures.
No neuron-based attribution graphs or comparison with replacement models.
No test of whether neuron explanations predict firing beyond the activating examples.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Neuron polysemanticity appears only as a cited background premise (ref. 10, Elhage et al.). The paper never inspects individual neurons, so it bears on no version. Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'assumes', and tranche from T5 to T6.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or estimate of the shares of one-job, two-job, or not-yet-understood neuron poles.
No neuron-pole share comparison across language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, or parameter scales up to trillions.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car analysis or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron shares under different tools or architectures, and no InceptionV1-sized vision-model comparison.
No attribution graphs or test of whether a model's own neurons suffice to explain behavior without a replacement model.
No test of whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict firing on new examples.
No automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.
